title: Spaghetti Aglio e Olio
subtitle: spaghetti with garlic, chilli and olive oil
excerpt: Spaghetti aglio e olio is a Roman pasta made from just five ingredients: garlic, dried chilli, flat-leaf parsley, black pepper and a generous amount of good olive oil, tossed with pasta cooking water to create a light emulsified sauce. The technique of toasting the garlic gently without burning it is what makes or breaks the dish. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Spaghetti aglio e olio is one of the most repeated examples of cucina povera, the Italian tradition of cooking with almost nothing. It is associated with Rome and Lazio but eaten across southern Italy as a late-night dish or a fast midweek meal. The dish is often made in the early hours after a night out, which is why it is sometimes called pasta di mezzanotte, midnight pasta.

glossaryTerms.definition: The Italian word for garlic, a foundational ingredient in Italian cooking used raw, roasted, fried and confit across all regions.
The Italian word for oil, almost always referring to extra virgin olive oil in a cooking context. Central to Italian cuisine at every level.

content.text: is a five-ingredient dish where the only technique that matters is toasting the garlic slices in warm oil until they are pale golden but not brown. Burnt garlic makes the whole dish bitter and there is nothing else to hide behind. Start the garlic in cold oil, raise the heat slowly and pull the pan off the heat the moment the edges turn gold. Serves 4.
Starchy pasta water is not optional here. It is what turns the olive oil from a coating into a light emulsified sauce that clings to every strand. Add it gradually and toss vigorously.

items.prepNote: finely sliced, or use dried flakes

content.text: Cook the spaghetti in a large pan of boiling water until just under al dente. Reserve at least 200ml of the cooking water before draining.

While the pasta cooks, put the garlic slices and olive oil in a cold frying pan. Set over medium-low heat. Cook slowly, swirling the pan occasionally, for 4 to 5 minutes until the garlic is pale golden at the edges. Add the chilli and cook for 30 seconds more. Remove from the heat immediately.
Add about 80ml of the pasta cooking water to the oil. It will spit and sizzle. Swirl to combine.
Add the drained pasta to the pan. Toss vigorously over medium heat for 1 to 2 minutes, adding more pasta water a splash at a time until the sauce is glossy and emulsified and coats each strand.
Remove from the heat. Add the parsley and black pepper, toss once more and serve immediately.

attrs.symptom: Garlic is bitter and too dark
attrs.cause: The heat was too high or the garlic was left for a few seconds too long
attrs.fix: Start in cold oil on low heat. Watch it the entire time and pull the pan off the heat the moment the edges turn pale gold

attrs.symptom: Pasta is oily rather than sauced
attrs.cause: Not enough pasta water was added or the tossing was not vigorous enough
attrs.fix: Add pasta water in small amounts and toss hard. The starch in the water is what creates the emulsion between the oil and water

attrs.symptom: Dish tastes flat despite garlic and chilli
attrs.cause: The olive oil was not good quality or the garlic was old
attrs.fix: Use your best extra virgin olive oil here. With so few ingredients, the quality of each one matters more than in any other dish

content.text: This pasta is made across southern Italy and Lazio, usually late at night. It is the dish you make when there is nothing in the house but a box of pasta, garlic, olive oil and a dried chilli. It takes 15 minutes from start to plate. In Naples it is sometimes called pasta aulive e chioppe, pasta with oil and capers. This version stays simple: garlic, chilli, parsley and pepper.
